attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: The firm 'will be' wording makes this a scorable forecast, although it reads partly as rhetorical exaggeration. 'By the time' sets the endpoint and is not a condition. The proposition is faithful.

contract.note: Treating 'all the Blackwells' as the cohort bought but not yet installed, and counting Rubin's age from commercial availability, are ordinary and fair readings. The contract correctly sets no calendar deadline.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's January 2026 statement of a planned Rubin availability window in H2 2026. It is a plan, not a record of actual availability, and says nothing about when Blackwell installation finished.
Dell's June 2026 blog post on the first Rubin rack delivery to CoreWeave. This is a company disclosure. It has no record of the Blackwell cohort finishing installation.

reviews.rationale: Rubin products began shipping around mid-2026, so Rubin could not be two years old before about mid-2028. Nothing in the packet shows the whole Blackwell cohort finished installing, so the early-resolution rule is not met. No deadline was stated, and the evidence cannot settle the outcome yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: This is a compound present-tense observation. The harm part is hedged with 'seems to', so it cannot be scored. 'Very little revenue' names no baseline. Only the claim that AI 'lacks tangible productivity benefits' is scorable in principle.

contract.note: The Q4 2025 period, the meaning of 'benefits' and the revenue baseline were all chosen by the evaluator, not the speaker. The support condition also requires evidence of harm, but under policy that hedged part should not be scored. These choices would decide any result.

evidence.note: A randomized trial run September to November 2025 finds AI gains on a workplace-style task. The setting is simulated, which the contract treats as context only. It is not proof of real workplace benefits.
METR's follow-up shows weak raw evidence of a speedup, but the authors call their own data unreliable because of selection effects. It settles neither the productivity part nor the harm part.

reviews.rationale: The harm part is hedged and cannot be scored, and 'very little revenue' has no baseline. The productivity part could be scored, but the packet only has simulated-task gains and a study its own authors call unreliable. Neither matches real workplace output in the contract period. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own estimate in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Comfortable estimating' is a confident estimate, not a hedge. The proposition keeps 'around 3GW' of IT load, the 3.9GW power conversion, and the speaker's own definition of capacity actually turned on.

contract.note: Using the speaker's own definition, operational IT load, with ordinary tolerance for an estimate is a fair plain reading.

evidence.note: CBRE measured 2.5GW of net absorption in primary markets in 2025. That covers only some markets and a different measure (net absorption), so it is near the estimate but not a match.

Cushman & Wakefield reports 3.9GW of colocation supply delivered across the Americas in H2 2025 alone. This points the other way, but it uses a different geography and measures delivery, not operational IT load.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no complete count of North American IT load that actually came online in 2025. CBRE measures net absorption in some markets only. Cushman & Wakefield measures Americas colocation deliveries. Neither confirms or refutes about 3GW of IT load, or the 3.9GW power figure.

attribution.note: Zitron's own calculation in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the FY2026 sales cohort and the 'around $44 billion' uninstalled figure. The figure is the speaker's estimate built from revenue shares and an analyst's cost per megawatt.

contract.note: Using fiscal year-end as the baseline and treating 'America' as US deployment are reasonable readings. The contract correctly says a wrong input alone does not make the estimate false.

evidence.note: The 10-K reports US revenue by where customers are headquartered, which may differ from where the hardware ships or is installed. It does not establish purchases for US deployment or any uninstalled balance.
The earnings release gives FY2026 Data Center revenue of $193.7B, not the $195.7B the speaker used. That corrects one input but measures revenue, not uninstalled hardware.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no matched records of sales, destinations and installation that would show how much FY2026 US-bound NVIDIA hardware was still uninstalled. One input is about $2B too high and the geographic basis is headquarters, not deployment. Neither fact settles the $44B estimate either way.
